div.head: Abt 9
div.ab: Gif frigman freum stelþ, III gebete, 7 cyning age þæt wite 7 ealle þa æhtan.
Gif frigman freum stelþ, III gebete, ⁊ cyning age þæt wite ⁊ ealle þa æhtan.
Gif frigman freum stelþ, III gebete, 7 cyning age þæt wite 7 ealle þa æhtan.
Wenn ein Freier einem Freien [etwas] stiehlt, büsse er [diesem] 3[fachen Werth], und der König erhalte die Strafsumme und alle die Güter [des Verbrechers].
If a freeman steals [something] from a freeman, let him compensate [him] 3[-fold value], and let the king receive the fine and all the goods [of the offender].
If a freeman robs a freeman, he shall pay a three fold compensation, and the king shall take the fine, or all [the man’s] goods.
If a freeman steals from a freeman, he is to pay three-fold, and the king is to have the fine or all the goods.
If a freeman steals from a freeman, let him pay 3[-fold], and the king obtains that fine or all the possessions.

note.seg: Die Form braucht nicht Plural zu sein, obwohl das Adj. substantiviert ist; auch untrumes ‘eines Kranken’ in Wi 6 ist stark dekliniert. Hier ist als Bestohlener nur der Gemeinfreie gemeint, denn der Adel war, wie laut 1. 4 König und Geistliche, im Eigentumschutz höher umfriedet

The form need not be plural, although the adj. is used as a noun; untrumes ‘of a sick man’ in Wi 6 is also declined strong. Only the common freeman is meant here as the victim of the theft, for the nobility, like king and clergy according to 1. 4, enjoyed a higher degree of protection for their property

Kardinales Zahlwort (s. d. Wb 4a) multiplikativ; Napier Lex. 94 s. v. þreo; M. Förster in Morsbach Festschr. 109⁴. Im Widerspruche mit dieser Busse (s. d. Gl 18) setzt pecunia .. furata .. saecularibus dupliciter Theodor Poenit. I 3, 2. Wie o. 1. 4. ist der Diebstahl nicht handhaft

Cardinal numeral (see that word in Wb 4a) used as a multiplicative; Napier Lex. 94 s. v. þreo; M. Förster in Morsbach Festschr. 109⁴. Contradicting this compensation (see that word in Gl 18), Theodore Poenit. I 3, 2 lays down pecunia .. furata .. saecularibus dupliciter. As above in 1. 4, the theft is not one caught in the act
Ich vermeide das Wort ‘Wette’, dem Ags. wed entspräche. — Gemeint scheint das Strafgeldfixum (s. d. Gl 3) von 12 Schilling
I avoid the word ‘Wette’, which would correspond to A.-S. wed. — What seems to be meant is the fixed fine (see that word in Gl 3) of 12 shillings

and steht öfter für ‘beziehungsweise’; s. d. Wb 2; auch Ine 74. Für ‘oder’ auch u. 87. Diese Bedeutung muss — wenn überhaupt die letzten vier Wörter nicht etwa spätere Interpolation (s. Gl Diebstahl 18a) nach strengerem Strafrecht sind — hier angenommen werden, da es Unsinn wäre, Konfiskation allen Vermögens neben Strafgeld zu fordern. Schwerlich ist zu ergänzen: ‘im Falle des Verbrechers Habe geringer ist als die Strafsumme’ (welchen Fall Hl 5¹ erwähnt; s. Wb: genoh); denn dass Fiskus einen Teil des verwirkten Geldes nahm, wo das ganze nicht vorhanden war, ist zu selbstverständlich. Vielmehr versteht Wilda (Strafr. 896) ‘und [im Falle handhaften Diebstahls]’; die Vermögenseinziehung (s. d. Gl 10 l) steht hierauf allerdings sonst auch. Dass and hier wie sonst (s. Gl Vermögenseinziehung 3d. 4f. 9) nur: ‘oder je nach Umständen, gemäss richterlichem Ermessen’ bedeute, geht nicht an, weil erstens einfachen Diebstahl in früher Zeit nicht Vermögenseinziehung trifft, und diese sich nie mit Busse an den privaten Kläger verbindet. — ‘Habe’ ist wohl hier nur die bewegliche. Dagegen verstehen ‘Gesamtvermögen’ Wilda 520. 846; Schmid 525

and often stands for ‘respectively’; see that word in Wb 2; also Ine 74. For ‘or’ also below 87. This meaning must be assumed here — unless indeed the last four words are perhaps a later interpolation (see Gl Diebstahl 18a) reflecting a stricter criminal law — since it would be nonsense to demand confiscation of all property in addition to a fine. It is hardly right to supply: ‘in case the offender’s goods are less than the penalty’ (a case mentioned in Hl 5¹; see Wb: genoh); for it is too self-evident that the fisc took part of the forfeited money where the whole was not available. Wilda (Strafr. 896), rather, understands ‘and [in the case of theft caught in the act]’; confiscation of property (see that word in Gl 10 l) is indeed laid down for this elsewhere too. That and here, as elsewhere (see Gl Vermögenseinziehung 3d. 4f. 9), means merely ‘or, according to circumstances, at the judge’s discretion’ is inadmissible, because, firstly, in early times simple theft does not incur confiscation of property, and confiscation is never combined with compensation to the private plaintiff. — ‘Habe’ [goods] here probably means only movable goods. Wilda 520. 846 and Schmid 525, on the other hand, understand ‘total property’

Liebermann takes and here as or (cf. cap. 87 below; Ine, cap. 27), since it would be pointless to exact a fine, where total confiscation was involved. He suggests that the choice between the two alternatives was determined by the gravity of the offence.

note.label: or
note.seg: As Liebermann suggests, the and in the text is probably used with an alternative sense. The king has all the goods if these are not enough to cover the fine.

note.label: possessions.
note.seg: Bill Griffiths, An Introduction to Early English Law (Norfolk: Anglo-Saxon Books, 1995), 33, translates: ‘the king shall take the fine and all the [stolen] goods.’ But it makes no sense to assume that the stolen goods would not be returned to the original owner. Following Liebermann and Whitelock, I take the second ⁊ here to be the adversative ‘or’ rather than the conjunctive ‘and.’ See parallels in §§23, 30, 80.
